content:
**Línea E: agent-runtime probe (#123) and the settings-hooks dedup (#315)**

Four PRs merged: #594 (#123), #613 (#315), #615 (#614), #621 (#616). Two follow-up tickets came from cold reviews of my own merged work.

What the tickets' premises got wrong, measured: #315 said the two compilers differed 'only in emit path'. They did not — 27 of 28 lines were byte-identical and the ONLY difference was the function name; the emit paths were separate exported constants that never sat inside the compiler. So the shared compiler takes no arguments, and the ticket's proposed compileSettingsHooks({emitPath}) would have injected a difference that does not exist. Emitted output md5 7d4dcb282df653b2121e98228e6ac569 for both, verified before deleting either copy.

The defects that reached main and needed follow-ups were all the same family: a reader collapsing distinct facts into one. probeAgentRuntime classified any spawn error as 'absent', so an installed-but-hung claude behind a proxy was told to install itself (#614). And the drift-guard for .gemini/settings.json compared against a working-tree file that antigravity.test.mjs rewrote on every run, so a mutated compiler wrote its own mutation into the evidence it would next be judged against: RED, GREEN, GREEN on three consecutive runs (#616). Note which guard: it was the settings one, NOT the AGENTS.md guard — AGENTS.md never had a test writing it, which is why #621 left that guard reading the working tree and said so in the file.

Three tooling lessons worth keeping. (1) 'git checkout --' does not revert an untracked file, and with a directory pathspec it exits 0 in silence, so a mutation-restore can leave the mutant on disk — mutation harnesses need byte backups with md5-verified restores. (2) A mutation harness with a hardcoded test target reports green because it never ran the test under study; two mutations in #621 did exactly that and had to be re-measured. (3) Two of my own new tests passed green with the protection removed: an mtime check that injected both seams itself (so it could never observe a write) and a 'teeth' test whose final assertion was byte-identical to the one above it. Cold review caught all three; none would have failed CI.

Also measured this session: memory capture does NOT require engram. 'npm run memory:share' fails on the missing binary, but MEMORY_BACKEND=plainfiles works — memory:save is pinned to plainfiles in package.json and its siblings are not. Four PRs declared capture impossible on that false premise. Filed as #641.

And one about the governance gate itself: CLOSING_RE is blind to negation. A PR body saying 'this does not fix #N' registers as closing #N — GitHub linked #645 to #641 that way. On the default branch 'Part of #N' alone is rejected outright, so a PR to main must close something.
